children: Cracker Barrel guided for sales to tick up this year as its new chief executive officer stands by a strategy put in place by his predecessor.

CEO David Deno, an industry veteran who joined Cracker Barrel last month, said the restaurant chain is already focused on the right areas and he is working to finetune its focus on food and customers.
"This company has been through a difficult stretch and has come out stronger," Deno said during a call with analysts. "The results of the past couple of quarters speak for themselves."

Deno succeeded Julie Masino, who oversaw a controversial rebranding campaign at Cracker Barrel that sparked widespread backlash. After everyone from die-hard customers to President Trump weighed in on the company's logo change, Masino walked back many elements of the strategy, and the business started showing signs of improvement before her exit.

Deno said he is looking to improve Cracker Barrel's food quality, focusing on dinner with upgrades to its chicken, hamburger and steak offerings. He also outlined plans to simplify product layouts and widen aisles in the company's retail shops while continuing to push more personalization in its loyalty program.
"A big part of my management philosophy is doing fewer things better," said Deno, the former CEO of Outback Steakhouse owner Bloomin' Brands.
"For restaurants, the formula is pretty straightforward. You must offer great food, provide a great guest experience, and hire and retain excellent employees who deliver both," he said.

For the full year ahead, Cracker Barrel said it expects revenue of about $3.33 billion to $3.4 billion, up from $3.32 billion for the year that ended July 31. Analysts polled by FactSet forecast $3.39 billion.
The company also expects comparable-store restaurant sales growth of 3% to 5%, and said it doesn't plan to open any new stores this year.
The stock rose 4.2% to $47.38, paring a gain of about 8% in premarket trading. Shares are now up about 87% year to date.
The guidance came after Cracker Barrel recorded higher profit in the fourth quarter and pointed to continued improvements in underlying traffic trends and some guest metrics.
Quarterly profit came in at $12.2 million, or 54 cents a share, compared with $6.75 million, or 30 cents a share, a year earlier.
Adjusted earnings per share were 99 cents, compared with analyst estimates of 17 cents, according to FactSet.
Revenue fell 2.2% year over year to $849.3 million, compared with analyst estimates of $834.6 million.
Comparable-store restaurant sales decreased 2.1%. Comparable store retail sales ticked up 0.7%.
